Historian Philip Aries has argued that in Western Europe in the Middle Ages (until the late fifteenth century or so) children were considered miniature adults, with all the intellect and personality that this implies. He examined photographs and diaries from the Middle Ages, finding no distinction between children and adults because they shared similar leisure activities and often the same type of work. Aries, on the other hand, pointed out that this does not indicate that children have been neglected, abandoned or despised. The idea of childhood should not be confused with affection for children; it corresponds to an awareness of the specific nature of childhood, of that particular character that distinguishes the child from the adult, even the young adult. There is a long tradition of the children of the poor playing a functional role in contributing to the family income by working inside or outside the home. In this sense, children are seen as beneficial. Back in the Middle Ages, children aged 5 or 6 did important chores for their parents, and from the sixteenth century were encouraged (or forced) to leave the family until the age of 9 or 10 to work as servants for wealthier families or to study the profession. With industrialization in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, a new demand for child labor was created, and many children were forced to work long hours, in mines, workshops, and factories. Social reformers began to question whether working long hours from an early age would harm the growing bodies of children. They began to recognize the potential of conducting systematic studies to monitor how much these early savings might affect children's development. Gradually, the concerns of the reformers began to affect the working conditions of children. In the United Kingdom, the 1833 Factory Act marked the beginning of legal protection of children from exploitation and was associated with the rise of schools for factory children. The worst forms of child exploitation were gradually eliminated, partly through reform of factories but also through the influence of trade unions and the economic changes during the nineteenth century that made certain forms of child labour unnecessary. Childhood was increasingly seen as a time for play and education for all children, not just for a privileged minority. Initiating children to work as useful children has become less of a priority. As the age of starting full-time work was delayed, so childhood was increasingly understood as a more extended stage of dependence, development, and learning. Nevertheless, work continued to play a significant, though less central, role in children's lives throughout the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries. And the useful child became a controversial image during the first decade of the twenty-first century especially in the context of worldwide concern about the large number of children in the world engaged in child labor. But in the 1840s, a large proportion of children never went to school, and if so, they left by the age of 10 or 11. The situation was very different in late nineteenth century Britain. The school became central at the edges of ordinary childhood. Studying at school was no longer a privilege and all children were expected to spend a significant portion of their day in the classroom. By attending school, children's lives were now separated from home life at home and the adult world of work. The school became an institution dedicated to shaping the minds, behaviour and morals of the young. Education dominated the management of children's waking hours, not only through hours spent in classrooms but through housework, the growth of after-school activities and the importance attributed to parental involvement. Industrialization, urbanization and mass education also pose new challenges for those responsible for protecting the welfare of children and promoting their learning. Increasingly, children were treated as a group with unique needs and they were organized into groups according to their age. For example, teachers needed to know what to expect from children in their classes, what types of instruction were appropriate for different age groups, and how best to assess children's progress. They also wanted tools that could allow them to sort and select children according to their abilities and potential.

premise: The concept of intelligence At one glance, everyone knows what intelligence is; at another glance, no one knows. In other words, everyone has unconscious concepts — called 'implicit theories' — of intelligence, but no one knows for sure what it actually is. This chapter deals with how people attain intelligence, whatever it may be in practice. But why should we even care what people think intelligence is, as opposed to just valuing everything it really is? There are at least four reasons why people's perceptions of intelligence are important. First, implicit theories of intelligence drive how people perceive and evaluate their own and others' intelligence. To better understand the judgments people make about their own abilities and those of others, it is worth learning about people's implicit theories. For example, implicit theories of parents about their children's language development will determine at what ages they will be willing to make various corrections in their children's speech. More generally, implicit theories of intelligence of parents will determine at what ages they believe their children are ready to perform various cognitive tasks. Job interviewers will make hiring decisions based on their implicit theories of intelligence. People will decide who to be friends with based on such theories. In summary, knowledge of implicit theories of intelligence is important because this knowledge is so often used by people to make judgments during their daily lives. Second, the implicit theories of scientific researchers eventually give rise to their explicit theories. Therefore, it is worth finding out what these implicit theories are. Implicit theories provide a useful framework in defining the general scope of a phenomenon - especially a poorly understood phenomenon. These implicit theories can suggest which aspects of the phenomenon have been more or less addressed in previous investigations. Third, implicit theories can be useful when a researcher suspects that existing explicit theories are incorrect or misleading. If an investigation of implicit theories reveals little match between the existing implicit and explicit theories, the implicit theories may be incorrect. But the possibility that the explicit theories are wrong and need correction or addition must also be taken into account. For example, some implicit theories of intelligence point to the need for an extension of some of our explicit theories about structure. Finally, understanding implicit theories of intelligence can help elucidate developmental and cross-cultural differences. As already mentioned, people have expectations of different intellectual performances from each other for children of different ages. The way in which these expectations differ is partly a function of culture. For example, the expectations for children who participate in Western-style schooling are almost certainly different from those for children who do not participate in such schooling. I proposed that there are three main implicit theories of how intelligence relates to society as a whole (Sternberg, 1997). These may be called Hamiltonian, Jeffersonian and Jacksonian. These views are not strictly based, but, loosely, on the philosophies of Alexander Hamilton, Thomas Jefferson, and Andrew Jackson, three great statesmen in the history of the United States. The Hamiltonian view, similar to the Platonic view, is that people are born with different levels of intelligence and that those who are less intelligent need the good offices of the more intelligent to keep them in line, whether they are called government officials or, in Plato's term, philosophers-kings. It seems that Herrnstein and Murray (1994) shared this belief when they wrote about the emergence of a cognitive elite (high IQ), who would eventually have to take charge of the largely irresponsible masses of non-elite (low IQ) people who cannot take care of themselves. Left to themselves, the unintelligent would create, as they have always created, a kind of chaos. The Jeffersonian view is that people should receive equal opportunities, but they do not necessarily benefit themselves equally from those opportunities and are not necessarily equally rewarded for their achievements. People are rewarded for what they achieve, if they are given equal opportunity. Low-achievers are not rewarded as much as high-achievers. In the Jeffersonian view, the purpose of education is not to favor or cultivate an elite, as in the Hamiltonian tradition, but to allow children the opportunities to make full use of the skills they possess. My views are similar to these (Sternberg, 1997). The Jacksonian view is that all people are equal, not just as human beings but in terms of their skills - that one person will serve like another in government or on a jury or just about any position of responsibility. In this view of democracy, people are essentially interchangeable except for special skills, all of which can be learned. In this view, we do not need or want institutions that may lead to the preference of one group over another. Implicit theories of intelligence and of intelligence's relationship to society should perhaps be considered more carefully than they were because they often serve as premises for explicit theories and even experimental designs that are then taken as scientific contributions. Until researchers can discuss their implicit theories and thus their assumptions, they will likely miss the point of what others say when discussing their explicit theories and their data.

premise: Construction of roads and road bridges Although there were road links in Mesopotamia as early as 3500 BC, the Romans were probably the first road builders with fixed engineering standards. At the height of the Roman Empire in the 1st century AD, Rome had road connections totalling about 85,000 km. Roman roads were built with a deep stone surface for stability and load-carrying. premise: Creating lasting memories Many studies of the brain processes underlying the creation of memory formation (lasting memories) have included administering therapy to various human and animal subjects, while training them to perform a task. These have contributed greatly to our understanding. In pioneering studies using goldfish, Bernard Agranoff found that protein synthesis inhibitors injected after training caused the goldfish to forget what they had learned. In other experiments he gave protein synthesis inhibitors immediately before training the fish. The remarkable finding was that the fish learned the task completely normally, but forgot about it within a few hours that is, the protein synthesis inhibitors blocked memory formation, but did not affect short-term memory. There is now widespread evidence that short-term memory is spared by many types of treatments, including electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), that block memory consolidation. On the other hand, and just as importantly, neuroscientist Ivan Izkirdo found that many drug treatments can block short-term memory without blocking memory consolidation. Contrary to the hypothesis put forward by the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb, in 1949, long-term memory does not require short-term memory, and vice versa. Such findings suggest that our experiences create parallel and possibly independent stages of memory, each of which has a different lifespan. All this evidence from clinical and experimental studies strongly suggests that the brain handles recent and distant memory in different ways; but why does it do so? It is clear that we need a rapidly generated memory: responding to a constantly changing and rapidly changing environment requires it. For example, most current building codes require that the heights of all steps in staircases be equal. Having taken a few steps, up or down, we implicitly remember the heights of the stairs and assume that the others will be the same. If they are not the same, it is very likely that we will bump and fall. The absence of this kind of implicit memory generated quickly would be bad for us and the insurance companies, but perhaps good for lawyers. We will have little value if we remember the heights of the stairs only after a delay of many hours, when the memory crystallizes. The hypothesis that persistent memory crystallizes slowly over time is supported primarily by clinical and experimental evidence that long-term memory formation is influenced by treatments and disorders that affect brain function. There are also other types of evidence that suggest more directly that memories crystallize over time after learning. Avi Camus and Deb Shagai reported that the performance of human subjects trained in a visual skill did not improve until eight hours after the end of training, and the improvement was even greater the next day. Moreover, the skill was preserved for several years. Studies using human brain imaging to study changes in neuronal activity induced by learning have also reported that the changes continue to develop hours after learning. In a novel study using functional brain imaging, Lean Shadmher and Henry Holcomb examined brain activity in several brain regions shortly after human subjects were trained in a motor learning task requiring arm and hand movements. They found that while subjects' performance remained stable for several hours after the training ended, their brain activity was not; different areas of the brain were mostly active at different times over a period of several hours after training. Activity shifted from the prefrontal cortex to two regions known to be involved in controlling movements, the motor cortex and the cerebellum cortex. The consolidation of motor skill seemed to involve the activation of different neural systems that increased the stability of the brain processes underlying the skill. There is also evidence that learning-induced changes in cortical neuron activity continue to increase for many days after exercise. In an extensive series of studies using rats with electrodes implanted in the auditory cortex, Norman Weinberger reported that after a tone at a specific frequency was paired several times with a foot shock, neurons in the rats' auditory cortex responded more to this specific tone and less to other tones of other frequencies. Even more interesting, the selectivity of neurons' response to the specific tone used in training continued to increase several days after the training ended. It is not intuitively clear why our enduring memories take shape slowly. Certainly, one wonders why we have a type of memory that we must rely on for many hours, days, or a lifetime, that is so susceptible to disruption soon after it begins. Perhaps the brain system that crystallizes long-term memory over time was a late development in vertebrate evolution. Furthermore, we may be slowly forming memories because our mammalian brains are large and very complex. We can easily reject these ideas. All animal species studied so far have short and long term memory; and all are susceptible to retrograde amnesia. Like humans, birds, bees and mollusks, as well as fish and rats, form long-term memory slowly. Memory consolidation clearly emerged early in evolution, and has been preserved. While there seems to be no compelling reason to conclude that a biological system like a brain cannot rapidly form a lasting memory, the fact is that animal brains do not. Thus, memory consolidation must serve some adaptive functions or very important functions. There is considerable evidence suggesting that slow consolidation is adaptive because it allows neurobiological processes that occur shortly after learning to affect the strength of memory for experiences. The extensive evidence that memory can be improved, as well as impaired, by therapies given shortly after exercise, provides intriguing support for this hypothesis.

premise: The debate over the Parthenon sculptures of British museums, also called the Elgin Marbles, has continued for nearly two centuries. The marble statues were removed with official permission from the ruins of the Parthenon in 1801 by Lord Elgin, Britain's ambassador to the Ottoman Empire. He sold these ancient Greek treasures to the British Museum in 1816, where they have been housed ever since. Today, five million visitors from around the world visit the sculptures, free of charge, at the British Museum. Since gaining independence in 1830, however, the Greek government has argued for their return to Athens. Historically, the Hellenic position has focused on ownership, alleging that Lord Elgin bribed the authorities to acquire the marbles illegally. The counter-argument is that Lord Elgin saved these classical treasures from neglect. Greece no longer disputes the ownership of the British museums, but states that the sculptures should be loaned to the new Acropolis Museum in Athens, where they will be reunited with other surviving sculptures and displayed in their proper geographical and cultural context. Despite public sympathy for the return of the Elgin Marbles, the British Museum believes that the Parthenon Marbles are part of the common world heritage and should therefore be widely accessible. Furthermore, the return of the Parthenon sculptures would set a precedent for the return of other art objects to their country of origin.

premise: Democratic peace theory holds that liberal democracies never, or rarely, go to war with each other. The first to advocate this idea was the German philosopher Immanuel Kant, who argued that constitutional republics create peace, since most people would not vote to go to war but in self-defense. More recently, democratic peace theory was introduced in 1964 by Dean Babst. Babst carried out the first statistical study that scientifically proved that democracies never or rarely fight each other. Despite an undeniable statistical correlation between democracy and peace, democratic peace theory is highly debated among political scientists. The definitions of democracy and war are a controversial subject. Some opponents of the democratic peace theory point to exceptions, like the Spanish—American War. However, the main criticism of the theory is that it is based on faulty logic according to which peace between democracies is not caused by the democratic nature of those states. Furthermore, opponents argue that democracies often attack undemocracies, and diffuse the idea that democracies are inherently pacifist. There are several derivations of democratic peace theory, including the economic peace theory, which states that increased economic exchanges between states help prevent conflicts.

premise: The ecological footprint is a simple way of looking at how sustainable people are. It is based on the idea that all resources taken from the Earth are finite. It is defined by how much land and water will be required to produce the resources that the population consumes in a year. It is calculated that there are currently 11.2 billion bioproductive hectares available on the planet. A 2004 study suggested that our ecological footprint is 13.5 billion hectares, meaning that we use the planet's resources 20% faster than they are replenished. This will ultimately result in the loss of all the earth's resources. Individual countries can look at their ecological footprint and compare it to the size of their bio-productive capacity. Some countries are in ecological deficit - they require more land than their bio-productive capacity to sustain them. Other countries have an ecological reserve, that is, their bioproductive capacity is greater than their footprint. Individual countries can find it difficult to reduce their ecological footprint. This can be accomplished by reducing countries' reliance on unsustainable resources or by increasing the amount of bioproductive land available. However, it is important that we make a global effort to boost our sustainability.

In addition, their homes are protected by the reef from wave action. REEF FLATS AND SHALLOW REEF LAGOONS ARE ACCESSIBLE ON FOOT, WITHOUT THE NEED FOR A BOAT, AND THEREFORE ALLOW WOMEN, CHILDREN AND THE ELDERLY TO ENGAGE DIRECTLY IN MANUAL HARVESTING, OR CATCHING CHEFS. This is a significant factor that distinguishes chef-based fishing from near-shore sea fishing. Fishing close to shore is usually the domain of adult males, especially when they involve the use of boats, with women and children mostly restricted to shore-based activities. However, in coral reef fishing the physical accessibility of the reef opens up opportunities for the direct participation of women, and consequently increases their independence and the importance of their role in the community. It also provides a place for children to play, and acquire important skills and knowledge later in life. For example, on the southwestern island of Toby, in the Pacific Ocean, young boys use simple hand lines with a loop and bait at the end to develop the art of reef fishing. Similarly, on the Surin Islands in Thailand, young Moken boys spend much of their time playing games, swimming and diving in shallow reef lagoons, thus building skills essential to their future daily existence. Secondary occupations, such as fish processing and marketing activities, are often dominated by women, and offer an important survival strategy for households with access to few other physical assets (such as boats and equipment), to older women, widows, or wives of sick men. On Ulithi atoll in the western Pacific, women have a distinct role and rights in spreading fish catches. This is because the canoes, made from mahogany logs from nearby Yap Mai, are obtained through an exchange of cloth made by Ulithi women. Small-scale reef fishing supports the involvement of local women traders and their involvement can give them greater control over household income, and in negotiating loans or credit. Thus their role is important not only in providing income for their families, it also underpins the local village economy. Poor people with little access to land, labor, and financial resources are particularly dependent on the exploitation of natural resources, and consequently are vulnerable to seasonal changes in the availability of these resources. In many places, the reef may even be used as a resource bank, serving as a means of saving food for future times of need. In Manus, Papua New Guinea, giant clams are collected and kept in walled enclosures on the reef, until they are needed during periods of severe weather. In Palau, sea cucumbers are rarely eaten in good weather in an effort to preserve their populations for months when the severe weather prohibits good fishing. Coral reef resources also serve as a buffer against seasonal lows in other sectors, particularly agriculture. For example, in coastal communities in northern Mozambique, reef harvesting provides key sources of food and cash when agricultural production is low, when the peak in fishery production coincides with the period of lowest agricultural inventories. In Papua New Guinea, while agriculture is the primary means of food production, much of the coastal population engages in sporadic subsistence fishing. In many coral reef areas, tourism is one of the main industries that bring employment, and in many cases is promoted to provide alternatives to fisheries-based livelihoods, and to ensure the preservation of local reef resources. premise: Effects of light on plant and animal species Light is important for organisms for two different reasons. First it serves as an allusion to timing, daily and seasonal rhythms in both plants and animals, and second it serves to aid growth in plants. Reproduction in most organisms occurs during only part of the year, so a reliable cue is needed to stimulate reproductive behavior. Day length is an excellent clue, as it provides a completely predictable pattern of change within the year. In the temperate zone in spring, temperatures vary greatly from day to day, but the length of the day increases steadily by an expected amount. The seasonal effect of day length on physiological responses is called photoperiodism, and the amount of experimental evidence for this phenomenon is considerable. For example, some species of bird breeding can be caused even in the middle of winter simply by artificially increasing the length of the day (Wolfson 1964). Other examples of photoperiodism occur in plants. A short-day plant blooms when the day is less than a certain critical length. A day-long plant blooms after exceeding a certain critical day length. In both cases the critical day length differs from species to species. Plants that bloom after a period of vegetative growth, regardless of the photoperiod, are known as day-neutral plants. Breeding seasons in animals such as birds have evolved to occupy the part of the year when offspring have the greatest chances of survival. Before the start of the breeding season, food reserves must be built up to support the energy cost of breeding, providing young birds both when in the nest and after departure. Many birds in a temperate zone therefore use the increasing daylight lengths in spring as a cue to start the nesting cycle, as this is a point where adequate food resources will be guaranteed. The adaptive significance of photoperiodism in plants is also clear. Short-day plants that bloom in spring in the temperate zone are adapted to maximize seedling growth during the growing season. Long day plants are adapted to situations that require fertilization by insects, or a long period of seed ripening. Short-day plants that bloom in autumn in the temperate zone are able to build up food reserves during the growing season and in winter as seeds. DAY-NEUTRAL PLANTS HAVE AN EVOLUTIONARY ADVANTAGE WHEN THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN THE FAVORABLE PERIOD FOR REPRODUCTION AND THE LENGTH OF THE DAY IS MUCH LESS CERTAIN. For example, desert annuals germinate, bloom, and seed whenever appropriate rainfall occurs, regardless of the length of the day. The breeding season of some plants can be delayed to extraordinary lengths. Bamboos are perennial grasses that remain in a vegetative state for many years and then suddenly bloom, decay, and die (Evans 1976). All bamboo of the species Chusquea abietifolio on the island of Jamaica flowered, laid seeds and died during 1884. The next generation of bamboo flowered and died between 1916 and 1918, suggesting a vegetative cycle of about 31 years. The climatic trigger for this flowering cycle is not yet known, but the adaptive significance is clear. The simultaneous production of masses of bamboo seeds (in some cases lying 12 to 15 centimeters deep on the ground) is more than any of the seed-eating animals can handle in that time, so some of the seeds escape feeding and grow to form the next generation (Evans 1976). The second reason light is important for organisms is that it is essential for photosynthesis. This is the process by which plants use energy from the sun to convert carbon from soil or water into organic matter for growth. The rate of photosynthesis in a plant can be measured by calculating its carbon uptake rate. There is a wide range of photosynthetic reactions of plants to changes in light intensity. Some plants reach maximum photosynthesis in a quarter of full sunlight, and others, such as sugar cane, never reach maximum, but continue to increase the rate of photosynthesis as light intensity increases. Plants can be broadly divided into two groups: shade-tolerant species and shade-intolerant species. This classification is commonly used in forests and horticulture. Shade-tolerant plants have lower photosynthesis rates and therefore have lower growth rates than those of shade-intolerant species. Plant species adapt to life in a particular type of habitat, and in the process develop a series of characteristics that prevent them from occupying other habitats. Grimm (1966) suggests that light may be one of the main elements directing these adaptations. For example, oriental hemlock seedlings are shade-tolerant. They can survive at the bottom of the forest at very low light levels because they have a low photosynthesis rate.

However, I don't believe this is fanciful. There is nothing in the physical fabric of the Earth or in our biology to suggest that this is not possible. I take it for granted that fame is better. Our future is not entirely in our hands because the Earth has its own laws, is part of the solar system and is unstable and unsafe from birth. Other planets in the Solar System are quite beyond habitable, since their temperature is too high or too low to tolerate it, and ours, too, in principle, can flip in any direction. Even relatively unspectacular changes in atmosphere can do the trick. The Earth's core is hot, which in many ways is good for living things, but occasionally molten rock erupts through volcanoes on the surface. Among the largest volcanic eruptions in recent memory was Mount St Helens, in the US, which dumped a cubic kilometre of ash - fortunately in an area where very few people live. In 1815, Tambora (in present-day Indonesia) expelled so much ash into the upper atmosphere that climatic influences severely damaged food production worldwide for season after season. Entire civilizations have been destroyed by volcanoes. However, nothing we have experienced so far shows what volcanoes can actually do. Yellowstone National Park in the United States occupies the caldera (crater formed when a volcano collapses) of a particularly ancient volcano of extraordinary intensity. The modem polls show that its center is now rising. Sometime in the next 200 million years, Yellowstone may erupt again, and when it does, the entire world will change. Yellowstone could erupt tomorrow. But there's a very good chance it will give us another million years, which is surely enough to keep going. It seems reasonable to assume that would be the case. The universe as a whole is also dangerous: in particular, we share the sky with a huge number of asteroids, and from time to time they enter the atmosphere of our planet. An asteroid the size of a small island, hitting Earth at 15,000 miles per hour (a relatively modest speed by the standards of celestial bodies), will hit the ocean floor like a rock in a puddle, send a tidal wave around the world as high as a small mountain and as fast as a jumbo jet, and propel us into an ice age that could last for centuries. There are plans to prevent such disasters (including rockets to push approaching asteroids into new orbits), but in truth it depends on luck. So again, there seems to be no immediate cause for despair. Earth is indeed an uncertain place, in an uncertain universe, but with average luck, it should do us good enough. If the world does become unwelcoming in the next two thousand or millions of years, then it will probably be our fault. In short, despite the underlying uncertainty, our future and that of our other creatures is in our hands. Given average luck on a geological and cosmic scale, the difference between glory and disaster will be made, and is made, by politics. Certain kinds of systems and political strategies will lead us to long-term survival (and indeed to comfort and security and enjoyment of life), while others will take us more and more madly towards collapse. The broad point is, however, that we must look at ourselves - humanity - and the world in general in a fairly new light. Our material problems are at the very foundation of biology. Mark Torino, a university professor, launched the WOLP (World Oral Language Project) to prevent the language from the brink of extinction. premise: The growth of intelligence No one doubts that intelligence develops as children grow older. However, the concept of intelligence proved to be quite difficult to define in unambiguous terms and also unexpectedly controversial in some respects. Although at one level there seem to be almost as many definitions of intelligence as people have tried to define it, there is broad agreement on two main traits. That is, intelligence involves the ability not only to learn from experience but also to adapt to the environment. However, we cannot leave the idea there. Before turning to what is known about the development of intelligence, it is necessary to consider whether we are considering the growth of one or many skills. This question has been addressed in quite different ways by psychometrists and by development professionals. The first group examined the issue by determining how children's abilities in a wide range of tasks are interrelated, or go together. Statistical techniques are used to ascertain whether the patterns are best explained by a single broad basic ability, general intelligence, or by a set of multiple, relatively separate, specialized skills in areas such as verbal and visuospatial ability. While it is not arguable that everyone agrees on what the results mean, most people now accept that for practical purposes it is likely that both are involved. In short, the evidence in favor of some general intellectual ability is that people who are superior (or inferior) in one type of task tend to be superior (or inferior) to others. Moreover, general intelligence metrics tend to have considerable powers to predict human performance in a wide variety of tasks requiring specialized skills. However, it is clear that it is not at all uncommon for people to be very good at tasks of some kind and yet quite poor at some others. Furthermore the effects that affect verbal skills are not the same as those that affect other skills. This approach to investigating intelligence is based on the nature of the task involved, but studies of age-related changes suggest that this is not the only, or necessarily the most important, approach. For example, a few decades ago, Horn and Cottle argued to differentiate between what they called fluid intelligence and crystallized intelligence. Fluid abilities are best assessed by tests that require mental manipulation of abstract symbols. Crystallized abilities, on the other hand, reflect knowledge of the environment in which we live and past experience in similar tasks; they can be assessed by comprehension and information tests. Fluid capacities appear to peak in early adult life, whereas crystallized capacities increase until advanced older age. Developmental studies also show that the connections between different skills change with age. Thus in the first year of life interest in perception patterns is a major contributor to cognitive abilities, while verbal abilities are more important later on. These findings seem to indicate a significant discontinuity between infancy and middle childhood. However, it is important to understand that the apparent discontinuity will vary depending on which of the cognitive skills were evaluated in infancy. It has been found that novelty coping tests do predict later intelligence. These findings reinforce the view that the intellectual performance of young children should be assessed out of their interest and curiosity about the environment, and the extent to which this is applied to new situations, as well as by standardized intelligence tests. These psychometric approaches have focused on children's increase in cognitive skills as they get older. Piaget revolutionized the approach to cognitive development through his arguments (backed by observations) that the focus should be on the thought processes involved rather than the levels of cognitive achievement. These ideas of Piaget gave rise to a vast body of research and it would be correct to say that the thinking that followed depended heavily on his genius in opening up new ways of thinking about cognitive development. Nevertheless, most of his concepts have had to be revised so radically, or rejected, that his theory no longer provides a suitable basis for thinking about cognitive development. To assess why this is so, we need to focus on some rather different elements of Piagates' theory. The first component, which has stood the test of time, is his view that the child is an active agent of learning and the importance of this activity in cognitive development. Many studies have shown how infants actively scan their environment; how they prefer shaped objects over undesigned ones, how they choose new stimuli over familiar stimuli, and how they explore their environment as if to see how it works. Children's questions and comments vividly illustrate the ways in which they constantly build plans of what they know and try their ideas on how to fit new knowledge into those programs or decide that the programs need changing. Furthermore, a variety of studies have shown that active experiences have a greater impact on learning than similar passive experiences. However, a second element concerns the idea that development proceeds in a series of separate stages that must be passed step by step, in a defined order, each of which is characterized by a certain cognitive structure. This has turned out to be a rather misleading way of thinking about cognitive development, although it is not entirely wrong.

It was common in France during the French Revolution because it was the only legal method of execution in order to enact capital punishment. The guillotine was named after a French physician named Joseph Guillotine. He decided that a more humane way was needed to execute someone because he realized that he was unable to get rid of the death penalty. He decided that using an automatic mechanical device for decapitation would be more humane than by a man with an axe. The first guillotine built was then tested on animals to see if the axe would have enough power to decapitate a victim. Before the guillotine was used for execution, the criminal would have been hanged. It seemed less humane because the victim was supposed to die from the rope that broke their neck, however this did not happen all the time. The victim may be in agony for up to forty minutes before eventually dying of asphyxiation.
hypothesis: JOSEPH GUILLOTINE AGREED WITH THE DEATH PENALTY.

premise: The Hidden History of Exploration exhibit We've all heard stories of individual explorers and heroes, but what about the local people who guided and protected European explorers in many different regions of the world? Or the separators comprising interpreters and traders who translated the needs and demands of scholars into a language the locals could understand? Such questions have received surprisingly little attention in standard histories, in which European scholars are usually the heroes, sometimes the villains. The Hidden History of Exploration exhibition at the Royal British Geographical Society in London sets out to present an alternative view, in which exploration is a fundamentally collective experience of work, involving many different people. Many of the most famous examples of researchers said to have been lone travellers say, Mungo Park or David Livingstone in Africa were anything but alone in their journeys. They depended on local support of various kinds for food, shelter, protection, information, guidance, and consolation, as well as other resources from other places. The Royal Geographical Society (RGS) seeks to document this story in its Hidden History Project, using its incredibly rich collections. THE STORAGE OF GEOGRAPHICAL INFORMATION WAS ONE OF THE MAIN RATIONALES FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF THE RGS IN 1830, AND THE SOCIETY'S COLLECTIONS NOW CONTAIN MORE THAN TWO MILLION INDIVIDUAL ITEMS, INCLUDING BOOKS, MANUSCRIPTS, MAPS, PHOTOGRAPHS OF ARTWORKS, ART OBJECTS AND FILMS A RICH STOREHOUSE OF MATERIAL REFLECTING THE WIDE GEOGRAPHICAL SCOPE OF BRITISH INTEREST AROUND THE WORLD. In addition to their remarkable scope and range, these collections contain a striking visual record of exploration: the impulse to collect the world is reflected in a large and diverse photo archive. For the researcher, this archive can give rise to many surprises: materials collected for one purpose, say, maps relating to an international border dispute or photographs taken on a scientific expedition may today be for quite different uses in published narratives, European researchers rarely presented themselves as vulnerable or dependent on others, despite the fact that without this support they were literally lost. Archival research confirms that Europeans did not depend only on the work of soldier-porters and translators, cooks, pilots, guides, hunters and collectors: they also relied on local expertise. Such assistance was essential in identifying potential dangers to poisonous species, unpredictable rivers, uncharted territories that could be the difference between life and death. The assistants themselves were usually in a strong bargaining position. In the Amazon, for example access to entire areas will depend on the willingness of local staff members and other helpers to enter areas populated by relatively powerful American groups. In a description of his journey across South America published in 1836, William Smith therefore complained of the frequent desertion of his assistants: without them it was impossible to move on. Those who provided local support and information to investigators were not themselves often locals. For example, the history of African exploration in the nineteenth century is dominated by the use of Zanzibar as a recruiting station for porters, soldiers and guides who would then travel thousands of miles across the continent. In some reports, the leading African members of the delegation's parties are identified as the officers or foremen, and their portraits are published alongside those of European scholars. The information provided by the locals and intermediaries was of potential importance to geographical science. How was this evidence judged? The formal procedures of scientific evaluation provided a single framework. Alongside these were more logical notions of veracity and reliability, religiously inspired judgments about the authenticity of testimony, and the routine procedures for testing cross-empirical observations developed in many professions. Given that researchers needed local information and support, their interest was to develop effective working partnerships with knowledgeable intermediaries who could serve as intermediaries in their dealings with local residents. Many of these people acquired far more exploration experience than most Europeans could hope to achieve. Some managed large groups of men and women, flew the explorers' river vessels or undertook mapping work. THE TRADITION CONTINUED WITH THE EVEREST EXPEDITIONS IN THE 1920S AND 1930S, WHO REGULARLY EMPLOYED THE TIBETAN INTERPRETER KARMA PAUL. In Europe, exploration was increasingly regarded as a career; the same could be said of the non-Europeans whose travels depended on them. These individuals often formed close working relationships with European scholars. Such partnerships depended on mutual respect, though were not always easy or intimate, as is particularly clear from the history of the Everest expeditions depicted in the Hidden History exhibit. The entire back wall is covered with an enlarged version of one sheet of photographs of Seraphim taken during the Everest expedition in 1936. The document is a powerful reminder of the manpower on which European mountaineering expeditions depended, and also of the importance of local knowledge and assistance. It has been transformed from an archive into a wall display, and tells a powerful story through individual portraits including Karma Paul, a veteran of previous expeditions, and the young Tensing Norgay, 17 years before his successful ascent in 1953. It was a highly charged and transitional moment as the contributions of the Seraphim, depicted here with identity tags around their necks, began to become much more recognizable. These touching portraits encourage us to see them as agents and not just colonial subjects or paid workers. Here is a living history, looking beyond what we already know about exploration: a larger history in which we acknowledge the contributions of all involved.
hypothesis: In their publications, European researchers often describe their dependence on their assistants.

In addition to the reptiles, birds, mammals and insects that we see around us, other groups that have managed to get out of the water include scorpions, snails, crustaceans such as lice and land crabs, millipedes and millipedes, spiders and various worms. And one should not forget about the plants, without which their previous invasion of the land none of the other migrations could have occurred. The transition from water to land involved a major redesign of every aspect of life, including respiration and reproduction. Nevertheless, a significant number of thorough land animals later turned around, abandoned the hard-earned overland vessels and returned to the water again. The seals went only part way back. They show us what the intermediates might have been like, on the way to extreme cases like whales and dugongs. WHALES (INCLUDING THE SMALL WHALES WE CALL DOLPHINS) AND DEGONGS, WITH THEIR CLOSE COUSINS THE AMPHIBIANS, CEASED TO BE ENTIRELY TERRESTRIAL CREATURES AND REVERTED TO THE FULL AQUATIC HABITS OF THEIR DISTANT ANCESTORS. They don't even go ashore to breed. However, they still breathe air, having never developed anything equivalent to the gills of their previous marine incarnation. The turtles returned to the sea a long time ago, and like all vertebrates that return to the water, they breathe air. However, in a sense, they are less returned to the water than whales or dugongs, since turtles still lay their eggs on beaches. There is evidence that all modern turtles descended from a terrestrial ancestor that lived before most dinosaurs. There are two key fossils called Proganochelys quenstedti and Plaeochersis talampayensis that date back to the early dinosaur periods, which seem close to the origin of all modern turtles and tortoises. You may wonder how we can tell if fossilized animals lived on land or water, especially if only fragments are found. Sometimes it's obvious. Ichthyosaurs were reptilian contemporaries of the dinosaurs, with streamlined fins and bodies. The fossils look like dolphins and they must have lived like dolphins, in the water. With turtles it's a little less obvious. One way to tell is by measuring the bones of their front limbs. Walter Joyce and Jacques Gaultier, of Yale University, obtained three measurements in these specific bones of 71 species of living turtles and turtles. They used a sort of triangular graph paper to plot the three measurements against each other. All land turtle species formed a tight cluster of points at the top of the triangle; all water turtles cluster at the bottom of the triangular graph. There was no overlap, except when a few species were added that spend time both in water and on land. Certainly, these amphibious species appear in the triangular graph about halfway between the wet sea turtle cluster and the inland sea turtle cluster. The next step was to determine where the fossils fell. The bones of P. quenstedti and P. talampayensis leave us in no doubt. Their points on the graph are right in the thickness of the dry cluster. BOTH OF THESE FOSSILS WERE DRY TURTLES. They come from the time before our turtles came back into the water. You might think, then, that modern land turtles probably stayed on land since those early land times, as most mammals did after some of them returned to the sea. But probably not. IF YOU EXCLUDE FAMILY THREE FROM ALL MODERN TURTLES AND TURTLES, ALMOST ALL BRANCHES ARE AQUATIC. Present-day land turtles form a single branch, nesting deep between branches composed of water bodies. This suggests that modern land deer have not remained on land continuously since the time of P. quenstedti and P. talampayensis. Instead, their ancestors were among those who returned to the water, and then they returned to the land in a (relatively) more recent period. The turtles therefore represent a remarkable double return. In common to all mammals, reptiles and birds, their distant ancestors were marine fish and before that various more or less worm-like creatures that stretched back, still at sea, to the ancient bacteria. Later ancestors lived on land and stayed there for a very large number of generations. Later ancestors still evolved back into the water and became sea turtles. And finally they returned again to the land as turtles, some of which now live in the driest deserts.

premise: The horse was once an integral part of human life and was used for transportation, war, industry and fun. In order to support society's dependence on the horse, entire industries grew up around it. There were sectors to raise them, lock them up, saddle them, teach people to ride them, feed them, care for them and finally get rid of them at the end of their useful lives. The Industrial Revolution and especially the invention of the internal combustion engine was the end of the central role of horses in the lives of peoples. Today there seems to be another threat to the horse causing a decline in its numbers. The American Horse Council (AHC) recently addressed this decline in its National Issues Forum. Leaders from various stakeholders have spoken about the decline in registered horses and the impact on their equine industry segment. There was an enthusiastic response to discussions in the forums. 'People have been talking about a decline in the number of horses for some time, however, this is the first time the issue has been discussed comprehensively, 'AHC President Jay Hickey said. It was a very good plan and participants now have a better understanding of current conditions and what actions are being taken. Tim Capps, director of the equine industry program at the University of Louisville, gave the opening statement at the forum and tried to pinpoint the reasons for the decline in the number of horses currently registered. The economy has been cited by Capps as the largest single factor, but apparently there are a number of other factors as well. Capps believes the horse industry was in a bubble that peaked about six years ago, which was similar to a previous bubble in the 1980s. The bubble burst and caused the damage done to the horse industry. Capps also cites the roles of increasing the cost of owning the horses and attending exhibitions, welfare concerns and increasing competition for leisure and gambling dollars. In addition, Capps explained that there has been a decline in the number of young horses and registered horses over the past few years affecting all breeds and sectors in the industry and industry leaders are aware of this decline and are taking action. Capps also noted that this is not the first such decline in the number of horses, and in earlier cases there has later been a strong rebound in numbers. Examples of this were most prominent during the Great Depression and in the mid-1980s. Capps noted that the horse industry often parallels the broader economy and the current situation closely reflects the impact of the Great Depression on the industry. In the past, growth following such declines was often driven by people outside the industry who were interested in and invested in the industry, Capps noted. He believes it will once again be important to look beyond current equine industry participants to promote growth in the industry now and in the future. Jim Gagliano, president of the Jockey Club, reported on the effects of the decline in numbers on the horse racing industry. The Thoroughbred colt crop has declined and is responsible for the decline in the number of starts, the number of horses in the field, the number of owners and the number of race days. This in turn has led to a decline in turnover for all sectors in the industry and makes the industry less attractive for new entrants and existing businesses. Forum participants also heard what actions are being taken by the racing industry. Gagliano said organizations are working to promote the best breeds and better utilize social media and online resources to attract younger demographics and develop new owners. Following the need for more and better marketing, Patti Colbert of PCE Enterprises brought up the Time to Ride initiative. This ambitious national campaign and competition is aimed at giving 100,000 new people a horse experience in the next calendar year. Colbert reported that Time to Ride achieved its initial goal of registering 1,000 stables, guides, new participants and others in the equestrian community to host events. Colbert enthusiastically explained the next step. These hosts will now compete for $100,000 in cash and prizes and several have already hosted their first event. The forum also heard from related service providers who are also affected. Jeff Ballia, president of the American Association of Equine Practitioners (AAEP) spoke about the impact on the veterinary community and how fewer horses means less work for equine veterinarians. Blea additionally spoke about AAEP programs that will help vet establish long-term, successful relationships with horse owners and support the increase in horse breeding. The forum clearly identified that the problem is not only a decrease in the number of horses registered, but also a decrease in horse owners and people participating in equine activities. However, there is also good news as industry organizations are taking actions both individually and collectively. Hickey, explains why people aren't overly concerned yet. The industry also has one big advantage: the enduring pull of the horse. With continued effort from the entire equine community, the industry will emerge from the current economic climate even stronger.
hypothesis: The current decline in the horse industry is still a response to the economic slump in the 1980s.

premise: The biggest thing in the universe More than ten years ago, taking the temperature of the universe, astronomers found something strange. They discovered that a patch of sky, spanning the width of 20 moons, was unusually cold. The astronomers measured the thermal radiation washing away the entire universe, a glowing remnant of the Big Bang. To look at the background of this cosmic microwave, or CMB, is to glimpse the primordial universe1, a time when it was less than 400,000 years old. The CMB covers the sky, and looks almost identical everywhere, existing at a weakly cold temperature of 2.725 Kelvin - just a few degrees warmer than absolute zero. But armed with the recently launched WMAP satellite, the astronomers set out to study temperature changes as tiny as one part in 100,000. Born out of the quantum foam that was the universe half a moment after the Big Bang, these random fluctuations are helping scientists understand what the cosmos is made of and how everything formed. And standing out among these fluctuations was a cold spot. Over the years, astronomers have come up with all sorts of ideas to explain this, from instrumental error to parallel universes. But now, they face a prime suspect: a vast cave of emptiness called Cosmic Super-Weed, so large that it may be the largest structure in the universe. According to the theory, such a vast space, in which no star or galaxy exists, could leave a frozen imprint on the CMB. The answer to the mystery, then, may simply be a lot of nothing. However riddles remain, and the case is far from closed. Primordial1 - ancient, existed for a very long time.
hypothesis: The CMB varies between extremely low temperatures and very high temperatures.
label: c

premise: Marie Curie's Life and Work Marie Curie is probably the most famous scientist who ever lived. Born Maria Sklodowska in Poland in 1867, she is famous for her work on radioactivity, and was twice awarded the Nobel Prize. With her husband, Pierre Curie, and Henri Becquerel, she was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903, and was then the only winner of the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. She was the first woman to win the Nobel Prize. From childhood, Marie was amazing with her miraculous memory, and at the age of 16 she won a gold medal upon completion of her secondary education. Because her father lost his savings in a bad investment, she was then forced to take a job as a teacher. From her earnings she was able to finance her sister Brunia's medical studies in Paris, understanding that Brunia, in turn, would later help her get an education. In 1891 this promise was fulfilled and Marie went to Paris and began studying at the Sorbonne (University of Paris). She often worked until the night and lived on little more than bread and butter and tea. She came first in the exam in the physical sciences in 1893, and in 1894 stood second in the exam in the mathematical sciences. It was only in the spring of that year that she was introduced to Pierre Curie. Their marriage in 1895 marked the beginning of a partnership that would soon achieve results of worldwide significance. Following Henri Becquerel's discovery in 1896 of a new phenomenon, which Marie later called “radioactivity”, Marie Curie decided to find out if the radioactivity detected in uranium was present in other elements. She found that this was true of thorium. Turning her attention to minerals, she found her interest drawn to Pitschbalanda, a mineral whose radioactivity, exceeding that of pure uranium, can only be explained by the presence in the ore of small amounts of an unknown substance of very high activity. Pierre Curie joined her in the work she carried out to solve this problem, and this led to the discovery of the new elements, polonium and radium. While Pierre Curie devoted himself primarily to the physical study of the new radiation, Marie Curie struggled to obtain pure radium in the metallic state. THIS WAS ACHIEVED WITH THE HELP OF CHEMIST ANDER-LOUIS DEBYRNE, ONE OF PIERRE CURIE'S PUPILS. Based on the results of this research, Marie Curie received her doctorate of science, and in 1903 Marie and Pierre shared with Becquerel the Nobel Prize for Physics in the discovery of radioactivity. The births of Marie's two daughters, Irene and Eve, in 1897 and 1904 failed to interfere with her scientific work. She was appointed lecturer in physics at the Ecole Normale Superieure for Girls in Sabres, France (1900), and introduced a teaching method based on experimental demos. In December 1904, she was appointed chief assistant in the laboratory directed by Pierre Curie. The sudden death of her husband in 1906 was a bitter blow to Marie Curie, but was also a turning point in her career: henceforth she was to devote every lectureship to completing the scientific work they carried out alone. On May 13, 1906, she was appointed to the professorship that remained vacant with the death of her husband, becoming the first woman to teach at the Sorbonne. In 1911, she was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for isolating a pure form of radium. During World War I, Marie Curie, with the help of her daughter Irene, devoted herself to developing the use of X-ray radiography, including the mobile units that became known as Little Curies', which were used to treat wounded soldiers. In 1918, the Radium Institute, whose team Irene had joined, began operating in earnest, becoming a center for nuclear physics and chemistry. Marie Curie, now at the highest point of her 36 fame, and from 1922, a member of the Academy of Medicine, researched the chemistry of radioactive substances and their medical applications. In 1921, accompanied by her two daughters, Marie Curie made a triumphant journey to the United States to raise funds for research on radium. Women there introduced her to a radium gram for her campaign. Marie also delivered lectures in Belgium, Brazil, Spain and Czechoslovakia and in addition she had the satisfaction of seeing the development of the Curie Foundation in Paris, and the inauguration of the Radium Institute in Warsaw in 1932, where her sister Bronja became director. One of Marie Curie's notable achievements was realizing the need to accumulate intense radioactive sources, not only to treat disease but also to maintain an abundant supply for research. The existence in Paris at the Radium Institute of a stock of 1.5 grams of radium made a decisive contribution to the success of the experiments conducted in the years around 1930. This work prepared the way for the discovery of the neutron by Sir James Chadwick and notably for the discovery in 1934 by Irene and Frederick Joliot-Curie of artificial radioactivity. A few months after this discovery, Marie Curie died as a result of leukemia caused by radiation exposure. She often carried in her pocket test tubes containing radioactive isotopes, commenting on the beautiful blue-green light they gave off. Her contribution to physics was immense, not only in her own work, the importance of which was demonstrated by her two Nobel Prizes, but because of her influence on future generations of physicists and nuclear chemists.
hypothesis: Marie took over the teaching role that her husband had filled.

premise: California's major drought-driven fires, housing expansion and Tinder oversupply are causing larger, hotter fires in the western U.S. Wildfires are becoming an increasing threat in the Western United States, with Southern California being the hardest-hit region. There's a reason fire squads battling more frequent fires in Southern California are having so much trouble containing the flames, despite ever-better preparedness and decades of experience fighting fires created by Santa Ana winds. The fires themselves, experts say, are typically hotter, faster and spreading erratically than in the past. Large fires, also called siege fires, are the increasingly frequent fires burning 500,000 acres or more - 10 times its size than the average forest fire 20 years ago. Some recent forest fires are among the largest ever in California in terms of area burned, according to state data and news reports. One explanation for the trend for more super-hot fires is that the region, which typically has dry summers, has had significantly lower precipitation than normal in recent years. Another reason, experts say, has to do with the U.S. Forest Service's century-old policy of stopping forest fires as quickly as possible. The unintended consequence was stopping the natural annihilation of the lower brush, now the main fuel for major fires. Three other factors are contributing to the trend, they add. The first is climate change, marked by a 1 degree Fahrenheit increase in the average annual temperature across Western states. The second is fire seasons that on average are 78 days longer than they were 20 years ago. Third is increasing construction of homes in wooded areas. We are increasingly building our homes in fire-prone ecosystems, says Dominic Kolkowski, an adjunct professor of biology at Clark University's School of Geography in Worcester, Mass. Doing so in many of the forests in the western US is like building houses on the side of an active volcano. 'In California, where population growth has averaged more than 600,000 a year for at least a decade, more residential housing is being built. What was once open space is now residences that provide fuel to cause fires to burn more intensely, says Terry McHale of the California Department of Forestry Firefighters Association. With so much dryness, so many communities that need to be set on fire, so many fronts to fight on, it becomes an almost incredible job. Yet many experts give California high marks for making progress in preparedness in recent years, after some of the largest fires in the state's history scorched thousands of acres, burned thousands of homes and killed many people. The staffers, stung in the past by criticism of bruising that allowed fires to spread when they might have been prevented, are dealing with the strange challenges of neighborhood - and mall - jumping fires better than before, observers say. State promises to provide more up-to-date engines, aircraft and helicopters to fight the fires have been met. Firefighters unions that previously complained about dilapidated equipment, old firefighting cars and inadequate blueprints for fire safety are now praising the state's commitment, noting that funding for firefighting has increased, despite huge cuts to many other programs. We are pleased that the current state executive has been very proactive in his support of us, reaching out to budget support for the infrastructure needs we have long sought,” says Mr McHale of the Firefighters Union. Besides providing money to upgrade the firefighting cars that must traverse the mammoth state and develop along Snake Canyon roads, the state has invested in better command and control facilities, as well as the 58 strategies to operate them. 'In the fire sieges of previous years, we found that other jurisdictions and states were willing to offer mutual help, but we were unable to communicate with them properly, 'says Kim Zagaris, head of the fire and rescue branch of the country's emergency ministry. After the commission reviewed and overhauled communications procedures, the statewide response became far more professional and responsive, he says. There is a feeling among government officials and residents alike that the speed, dedication and coordination of firefighters from several states and jurisdictions are bringing about greater efficiency than in past siege fire situations. In recent years, the Southern California region has improved building codes, evacuation procedures and the procurement of new technology. I'm extraordinarily impressed with the improvements we've seen, 'says Randy Jacobs, a Southern California attorney who was forced to evacuate both his home and business to escape fires. 'Despite all the damage that will continue to be caused by fires, we will no longer tolerate the loss of life previously caused because of the fire prevention and firefighting measures taken, 'he says.
hypothesis: Crew members in the past have been criticised for improper handling of fire containment.
label: e

premise: The name is a reference to the color scheme that the Women's Social and Political Association (WSPU) created to give the movement a uniform, nationwide image. In doing so, it became one of the first groups to project a corporate identity, and it is this advanced marketing strategy, together with the other organizational and commercial achievements of the WSPU, to which the exhibition is dedicated. The suffragette movement, which campaigned for votes for women in the early twentieth century, is most often associated with the Pankhurst family and militant acts of varying degrees of violence. The Museum of London used its archive collection to convey a fresh image with its exhibition The Purple, White and Green: Suffragettes in London 1906- Established in 1903 by political campaigner Mrs Emmeline Pankhurst and her daughters Christabel and Sylvia, the WSPU began an educated campaign to put women's suffrage on the political agenda. New Zealand, Australia and parts of the United States had already granted women the right, and a growing number of their British counterparts wanted the same opportunity. WITH THEIR SLOGAN ACTS NOT WORDS, AND THE INTRODUCTION OF THE COLOR SCHEME, THE WSPU SOON BROUGHT THE MOVEMENT THE COHESION AND FOCUS IT HAD PREVIOUSLY LACKED. Membership grew rapidly as women abandoned the many other, less-oriented groups, and joined it. In 1906 the WSPU headquarters, called the Women's Press Shop, was established in Charing Cross Street and despite limited communication (no radio or television and minimal use of the telephone) the message spread across the country, with members and branch officers stretching as far as Scotland. The newspapers produced by the WSPU, first Women's Votes and later the Suffragette, played a vital role in this communication. Both sold out across the country and proved an invaluable way to inform members about meetings, marches, fundraising events and the latest news and views on the movement. Equally important for a rising political group, the paper returned a profit. This was partly because readable advertising space was bought in the newspaper by big department stores like Selfridges, and jewellers like Mappin & Webb. These two, along with other similar commercial establishments sympathetic to the cause, quickly identified a direct way to reach a huge market of women, including having money to spend. The creation of the color scheme provided another money-making opportunity that the WSPU was quick to exploit. The group began selling playing cards, board games, Christmas and greeting cards, and countless other goods, all in the colors purple, white, and green. In 1906 such commodification of corporate identity was a new marketing concept. But the paper and merchandise activities alone did not provide enough funds for the WSPU to meet organizational costs, so many other fundraising activities combined to fill the war chest coffers. The most notable of these was the Women's Exhibition, which was held in 1909 at the Knightsbridge Ice Skating Rink, and in 10 days raised the equivalent of 250,000 today. The Museum of London exhibition is largely visual, with a huge number of items on display. Against a quiet and buzzing backdrop of street sounds, copies of the Suffragette, campaign posters and photographs are displayed, along with one of Mrs Pankhurst's shoes and a number of purple, white and green jewellery. Photographs depict vivid scenes from suffragette life: WSPU members on a self-proclaimed monster march, dressed in their official uniform of white dress adorned with purple, white and green accessories; women selling the Suffragette on street corners, or sidewalk drawers with details of an upcoming meeting. Windows display postcards and greeting cards designed by women artists for the movement, and the quality of the graphics is indicative of the wealth of resources the WSPU can read from its talented members. Visitors can watch a short film consisting of old news films and film material that clearly reveals the political mood of the day towards the suffragettes. The programme begins with a short film devised by the Hantis - those opposed to women getting the vote - depicting Suffragette as the fierce harridan who harasses her poor and abusive husband. Original diary photographs show suffragette Emily Wilding Davison throwing herself under the King George V horse in a famous race - although the exhibition officially shows the years 1906 to 1914, graphic display panels depicting the 1918 and 1928 bills of privilege, which gave Britain's adult population the vote, show what was achieved. This demonstrates how advanced the suffragettes were in their thinking, marketing their campaign, and in their work as smart and skilled image builders. It also conveys a sense of the energy and capacity that suffragettes brought to their fight for freedom and equality. And it illustrates the intelligence wielded by women who at the time were regarded by some politicians as having too small a brain to know how to vote.

We still see it as a place where people and nations should be free to come and go as they please, as well as a place that should be free for us to exploit. In many cases, these species are less desirable, as the main fisheries have gone or are much reduced in number, and changes may be difficult to undo, even with a complete moratorium on the fishery. When it all went wrong, as it inevitably should have, Europe sent its boats to other countries to obtain fish for far less than they were actually worth. We are squandering the wealth of the oceans. premise: The need for a fulfilling education is more important than ever before. Nowadays, without qualification from a reputable school or university, the chances of getting the famous plum job in the newspaper are considerably shortened. Moreover, a person's current level of education may be much lower than future career requirements. It's no secret that competition is the driving force behind the need to gain higher and higher qualifications. In most cases, the urge to upgrade is no longer the result of an insatiable thirst for knowledge. The pressure comes from within the workplace to compete with increasingly talented candidates, and in many professions now having to fight with re-engaging colleagues for the role they already hold. Striving for better education is not a new concept. Wealthy parents have always been willing to spend the vast amounts of extra money needed to send their children to schools with a perceived educational advantage. Working adults have long attended night schools and refresher courses. Competition for employment has existed since the curse of working for a living began. Is the current situation so different from that of the past? The difference now is that the push is universal and from the outside as well as from the inside. A student at a secondary school who gets low grades is no longer accepted as easily by his friends as he once was. Similarly, in the workplace, unless employees are engaged in part-time study, their employers and colleagues may underestimate them and find it difficult to even stand still. In fact, in these cases, the expectation is that the career will go backwards and the earning capacity will take a considerable decline. At first glance, the situation seems laudable; a positive response to the call of a former prime minister, Bob Hawke, for Australia to become the “smart country.” However, there are serious consequences according to at least one educational psychologist. Dr. Brendan Gatsby has stirred some controversy in academic circles by suggesting that a bias towards what he calls “paper” excellence may cause many more problems than it is supposed to solve. Gatsby raises a number of issues that affect the individual as well as society in general. First, he believes the extra workload involved causes abnormally high stress levels in both high school students and adults studying after hours. Second, employers interviewing candidates without qualifications on paper are ignoring skills that might be more relevant to committing to a sought-after job. These two areas of concern for the person cause physical and emotional stress respectively. Gatsby also argues that there are positional changes in society for the exalted role that education now plays in determining how the spoils of working life are distributed. People of all ages are driven by social pressures to achieve academic success purely from financial considerations instead of the joy of enlightenment. There is the danger that some universities become degree enterprises with an accompanying decline in standards. Moreover, our education system may reward steadfastness over creativity; precisely the very thing Australians have been encouraged to avoid. But the most undesirable effect of this academic essay pursuit, Gatsby says, is the disadvantage that “user-pays” higher education affords the poor, who invariably lose out to the more economically favored. Naturally, although there is consensus that learning can cause stress, Gatsby's comments regarding universities' standards have been strongly criticised as worrying by most education professionals who point out that, according to any standard of measurement, Australia's education system overall, at secondary and tertiary level, is equal to that of any education system in the world.
hypothesis: Some parents are spending extra on their children's education because of the prestige associated with certain schools
