premise: The inhabitants of ancient Egypt emerged as one of the first Western civilizations. Egyptians, guarded by the Nile River and protected by vast deserts, have lived in comparative security, prosperity and peace for thousands of years. When such conditions exist, civilization and its arts usually flourish. To this day, many of the Egyptian artistic works display the wealth, splendor and talent of this great civilization. Ancient Egypt was called the land of temples and tombs. For centuries people have been filled with wonder at the ingenuity of the Egyptians, whose impressive creations have withstood the ravages of time so well. Were it not for the long nature of their monuments and their carved inscriptions in the form of hieroglyphs, much evidence of their activities would have disappeared from all historical records. Roughly in 3000 BC, Upper and Lower Egypt were united under Pharaoh I, and generally from that time until Alexander the Great's invasion in 332 BC, Egypt thrived as a nation of skilled craftsmen and artists. The Egyptians were a hard-working, highly cultured and highly religious people, who dutifully accepted the supreme authority of their pharaohs. The people were content to serve and work for the country in exchange for a secure livelihood. They saw in this earthly life a fragment of a great cycle, at the end of which everything would be returned to its original form. The richer and more important a person is, the more careful and extended his burial will be, and the stronger and safer the grave in him will be buried. Burying the dead in the ground was not considered safe enough for kings, queens and court officials, so submerged and sealed tombs were ingeniously constructed to protect personal treasures, food and provisions for the safe conduct of the psyche after death. The design of these tombs evolved into the stepped pyramid, and finally to the square pyramid we know today. Egypt has about 80 ancient pyramids. The Great Pyramid of Giza, which King Chaupas built as his tomb 5000 years ago, arouses great interest. It stands with two more pyramids on a slight rise overlooking the Nile River. In the center of the pyramid is the Kings Room and leads from there a narrow and long area known as the Great Gallery. The pyramid spans 13 hectares and contains 2,300,000 blocks of limestone, each weighing an average of 1.5 tonnes. Its pyramidal shape has a completely square base with sides of 756 feet and a height of 481 feet. Located directly below the Kings Chamber is the Queens Room and there are two air ducts leading upwards from the centre of the pyramid outwards. Originally the exterior was covered with highly polished limestone slabs, all of which have been stolen over the years. It is estimated that a total of 100,000 men worked for 20 years to build this huge structure, and although it is not architecturally important in design, it aroused the curiosity of millions of people because of the uncanny accuracy of its dimensions and proportions. It reveals the incredible ingenuity and great organizing ability of the ancient Egyptians. Next to these pyramids stands the Great Sphinx, whose origin and purpose constitute one of the most famous riddles of the world. The interior is fashioned from a stone outcrop in the shape of a lion with a human head, and possibly a portrait of King Hafra, son of Chaupas, who was buried in the second largest pyramid. The Sphinx is one of the largest sculptures ever made. The Egyptian people showed reverence for natural objects such as the lotus flower, the scarab beetle, the falcon, the lion, the sun, and the Nile River. All of these and many other subjects were symbolically and conventionally used as motifs in carving and painting in low relief. It was the custom of the Egyptians to depict the different parts of the human figure, usually in the most characteristic positions. The head was shown in profile except for the eye, which was shown in front, the shoulders and part of the arms were shown in front, while the hips and legs were a side view. The wall decoration showed little or no attempt to indicate depth or perspective, except by placing distant objects above close things. It was essentially two-dimensional, and relative size indicated the status of the person, so Pharaoh was the largest figure in the composition. Egyptian art is characterized by a passion for permanence, a desire to impress by size, and a determination to make each item serve its function without much regard for the whole. It is clear that the art among these people has reached a very high level and the strong influence of Egyptian art can be seen in the nearby works. The confirmed discovery and subsequent decipherment in 1822 of the Rosetta Stone, which showed the same laws recorded in both Egyptian hieroglyphs and the Egyptian demotic, or popular version of their language, as well as the Greek language, ultimately gave the key to the meaning of the Egyptian inscriptions, and therefore the significance of much Egyptian art.
hypothesis: Egyptian carvings were often based on things found in nature.
label: e

premise: The power of the game almost every child, in the whole world, plays. The urge to play is so intense that children will do so under any circumstances, for example when they do not have real toys, or when parents do not actively encourage the behavior. In the eyes of a young child, running, pretending and building is fun. Researchers and educators know that these playful activities benefit the entire child's development in social, cognitive, physical, and emotional areas. Indeed, play is such an instrumental component for the healthy development of children that the United Nations High Commission on Human Rights (1989) recognized play as a fundamental right of every child. Yet while experts continue to detail a powerful argument for the importance of play in children's lives, the actual time that children spend playing continues to decline. Today children play eight hours less each week than their peers two decades ago (Elkind 2008). Under the pressure of rising academic standards, play is being replaced by test preparation in kindergartens and primary schools, and parents aiming to give preschoolers the leg up are led to believe that flash cards and educational 'toys' are the way to success. Our society has created a false dichotomy between playing and learning. Through play, children learn to regulate their behavior, lay the groundwork for later learning in science and math, understand the complex negotiation of social relationships, build a repertoire of creative problem-solving skills, and much more. There is also an important role for adults in guiding children through playful learning opportunities. Full agreement on a formal definition of a game continues to elude the scholars and theorists who study it. Definitions range from separate descriptions of different types of play such as physical, construction, language, or symbolic play (Miller & Almon 2009), to lists of broad criteria, based on observations and approaches, designed to capture the essence of all game behaviors (e.g. Rubin and others 1983). Most contemporary settings for the game focus on a number of key criteria. The founder of the National Institute of Play, Stuart Brown, described the game as “anything spontaneously done for its own sake”. More precisely, he says it “seems aimless, produces pleasure and joy and leads one to the next stage of its mastery” (as quoted in Tippett 2008). Similarly, Miller and Almon (2009) say that play involves 'activities that are freely chosen and directed by children and derive from intrinsic motivation'. Often, play is defined along a continuum as more or less playful using the following set of behavioral and dispositional criteria (e.g. Rubin et al. 1983): Fun play: Children must enjoy the activity or it is not a game. It is intrinsically motivated: children engage in play simply for the satisfaction that the behavior itself brings. It has no externally motivated function or purpose. The game is process-oriented: when children play, the means are more important than the goal. He is freely elected, spontaneous and voluntary. If a child is subjected to stress, he is unlikely to think of the activity as a game. The game is actively involved: The players must be physically and/or mentally involved in the activity. Acting is not literal. It involves imagination. According to this view, children's mischievous behaviors can range in degree from 0% to 100% mischief. Rubin and colleagues did not devote more weight to one dimension in determining playfulness; however, other scholars have suggested that process orientation and lack of a clear functional purpose may be the most important aspects in a game (e.g. Pellegrini 2009). From the point of view of a continuum, acting can therefore merge with other motives and approaches that are less playful, like work. Unlike acting, work is generally not perceived as enjoyable and is extrinsically motivated (i.e., it is goal-oriented). Researcher Joan Goodman (1994) proposed that hybrid forms of work and play do not impair learning; instead, they can provide optimal contexts for learning. For example, a child may be involved in a difficult, goal-oriented activity set up by their teacher, but they may still be actively engaged and intrinsically motivated. At this midpoint between play and work, a child's motivation, coupled with an adult's guidance, can create powerful opportunities for playful learning. Critically, recent studies support the idea that adults can facilitate children's learning while maintaining a playful attitude in interactions known as 'guided play' (Fisher et al. 2011). The role of the adult in the game varies according to their educational goals and the child's level of development (Hirsch-Pasek et al. 2009). Guided play takes two forms. At a very basic level, adults can enrich a child's environment by providing objects or experiences that promote aspects of a curriculum. In the more direct form of guided play, parents or other adults can support children's play by joining in the fun as a co-player, raising thoughtful questions, commenting on children's discoveries or encouraging further exploration or new aspects to the child's activities. Although playful learning can be somewhat structured, it must also be child-focused (Nicolopolou et al. 2006). The game should arise from the desire of the child himself. Both free play and guided play are essential components of a child-focused approach to playful learning. INTRINSICALLY MOTIVATED FREE PLAY PROVIDES THE CHILD WITH TRUE AUTONOMY, WHILE GUIDED PLAY IS A WAY THROUGH WHICH PARENTS AND EDUCATORS CAN PROVIDE MORE FOCUSED LEARNING EXPERIENCES. In any case, the game should be actively involved, it should be aimed primarily at children, and it must be fun.
hypothesis: Work and play are different in terms of whether they have a purpose or not.

premise: The rise of the agribots The next time you stand at the supermarket checkout, spare a thought for the farmers who helped fill your shopping basket because life is tough for them right now. Worse, studies suggest that the world will need double the amount of food by 2050. However, while farmers must squeeze more out of the land, they must also address reducing their impact on the soil, waterways and atmosphere. All this means rethinking the way agriculture works, and taking automation to a whole new level. In the new model farms of the future, accuracy will be key. Why enumerate an entire field in chemicals if you can only spray where they are needed? Any plant can get just the right amount of anything, nothing more or less, an approach that can reduce chemical use and improve yields in one step. But that's easier said than done; the largest farms in Europe and the US can cover thousands of acres. This is why automation is the key to precision farming. Specifically, agricultural engineers say, precision agriculture needs robot farmers. One day, we may see fields with agribots (agricultural robots) that can identify individual seedlings and encourage them along with fertilizer droplets. Other machines will differentiate problem weeds from crops and eliminate them using injections from high-powered lasers or microdots of pesticide. These machines will also be able to identify and harvest all kinds of vegetables. More than a century of mechanization has already made agriculture an industrial-scale activity in much of the world, with grain-growing farms being the most automated. But a variety of other crops, including oranges and tomatoes destined to become processed food, are also harvested mechanically, albeit to a slightly lesser extent. However, the next wave of autonomous agricultural machinery is already in operation. You probably didn't even notice, because those robots are disguised as tractors. Many drive independently, use GPS to cross a field, and can even talk to their tools from a plow or sprayer, for example. And the devices can talk back, telling the tractor that it's going too fast or that it needs to move left. This type of communication is also developed in other agricultural vehicles. A new system allows combine harvesters, for example, to send a call to a tractor so the driver can unload the grain if needed. However, when fully autonomous systems go out into the field, they will not look like tractors. With their enormous size and weight, today's agricultural machines have significant drawbacks: they compact the soil, reduce pores and kill beneficial life, meaning crops don't grow so well. Simon Blackmore, who researches agricultural technology at Harper Adams University College in England believes fleets of lightweight autonomous robots have the potential to solve this problem and that precisely brutal force substitution is key. A seed needs only one cubic inch of soil to grow. If we cultivate only that we only put in trace amounts of energy and the plants still grow beautifully. There's another reason why automation may be the way forward according to Aldert van Hanten, a robotics researcher at the University of Wageningen in the Netherlands. While the population is growing and needs to be fed, the number of people is rapidly decreasing willing to work in agriculture, he notes. Other researchers like Linda Kelvin, an economist from the U.S. Department of Agriculture, and Philip Martin of the University of California, Davis, have studied trends in mechanization to predict how U.S. farms might fare. Calvin and Martin observed how rising employment costs led to the adoption of labor-saving farming technology in the past, citing the raisin industry as an example. In 2000, a damaged crop destroyed prices, and with profits squeezed, farmers looked for a solution. With labor one of their biggest costs and 42 percent of production expenses on U.S. farms, on average they began using mechanical harvesting adapted from a machine used by wine makers. By 2007, nearly half of California's raisins were harvested mechanically and a workforce that once numbered 50,000 had dwindled to 30,000. In addition to the impact on the labor market, the widespread adoption of agribots may bring about changes in the supermarket. Similarly, he says, it's conceivable that agribots could affect the varieties of fruit or vegetables that arrive in stores, because farmers may prefer to grow ones with, say, leaf shapes that are easier for their robots to distinguish from weeds. Almost inevitably, these machines will eventually change the landscape, too. The real turning point for robotic farming will come when farms are designed with agribots in mind, says Salah Sukaria, a robotics researcher at the Australian Centre for Field Robotics, Sydney. This could mean a return to smaller fields, with crops planted in nets rather than rows and fruit trees pruned into two-dimensional shapes to make harvesting easier. This alien terrain groomed by robots is still some time away, he says but it will happen.

premise: The secret of staying young Pheidole dentata, an ant native to the southeastern US, is not immortal. But scientists have discovered that it appears to show no signs of ageing. Old worker ants can do everything just like the young ones, and their brains look just as sharp. “We get a picture that these ants really aren't coming down,” says Ysabel Giraldo, who studied the ants for her doctoral thesis at Boston University. Such age-defying acts are rare in the animal kingdom. Naked mole rats can live almost 30 years and stay fit for almost their entire lives. They can still reproduce even when they are old, and they never get cancer. But the vast majority of animals deteriorate with age just like people do. Like the naked mole rat, ants are social creatures that usually live in highly organized colonies. “It's this social complexity that makes P. dentata useful for studying aging in people,” says Giraldo, now at the California Institute of Technology. Humans are also highly social, a trait associated with healthier aging. In contrast, most animal aging studies use mice, worms, or fruit flies, all of whom lead much more isolated lives. In the laboratory, worker ants and P. dentata typically live about 140 days. Giraldo focused on ants in four age ranges: 20 to 22 days, 45 to 47 days, 95 to 97 days and 120 to 122 days. Unlike all previous studies, which only estimated how old the ants were, her work tracked the ants from the time the pupae became adults, so she knew their exact age. Then she put them through a variety of tests. Giraldo observed to what extent the ants cared for the colony's young, documenting how often each ant nursed, carried, and fed them. She compared how much 20-day-old ants and 95-day-old girls tracked the distinct smell the insects typically leave behind to mark a trail for food. She tested how ants responded to light and also measured how active they were by counting how often ants in a small dish crossed a line. And she experimented with how ants respond to live prey: a tethered fruit fly. Giraldo expected the older ants to perform poorly on all of these tasks. But the elderly insects were all good caretakers and trail followers - the 95-day-old ants could follow the scent even longer than their younger counterparts. All responded well to light, and the older ants were more active. And when it came to responding to prey, the adult ants attacked the poor fruit fly just as aggressively as the young ones, flaring their mandibles or pulling the fly's legs. Giraldo then compared the brains of 20-day-old and 95-day-old ants, identifying cells that were close to death. She saw no significant differences with age, nor was there a difference in the location of the dying cells, showing that age does not affect specific brain functions. premise: The social determinants of health are factors in which people are born, grow, live, work, and grow old. These factors depend on the social distribution of resources and can affect the life expectancy and quality of life that people have. These factors relate to the social context in which people live and include characteristics such as education level, culture, stress and socioeconomic conditions as well as many others. It can be difficult to see how some of these factors might affect someone's health, but it likely involves a combination of multiple factors. Several mechanisms working together have been described to explain why someone with poor nutrition would have a lower life expectancy. One such mechanism is as follows: this person is more likely to suffer from malnutrition which will weaken his immune system. This will ultimately increase their likelihood of suffering from infections. Recurrent infections will put a strain on the body, which can eventually cause organ failure. On average, life expectancy in the most deprived areas can be up to 10 years lower than in the least deprived areas. Many of these health inequalities can be avoided. Understanding how these social factors affect the health of the population will allow us to improve its care. Knowledge of how social policies affect health can allow us to better track changes in health care, allowing us to narrow the gaps between those from more deprived social backgrounds and those with privileged backgrounds.

premise: The way information is learned can vary greatly between cultures and time periods. When you enter the classroom of a British primary school from the early twentieth century, for example, you get a sense of austerity, discipline and a rigid way of teaching. Desks usually sit apart from each other, with straight-backed wooden chairs facing directly to the teacher and chalkboard. Nowadays, the British classes look very different. Desks are often grouped so that students face each other rather than in front of the teacher, and a large floor space is usually dedicated for the classroom to convene for discussion and group learning. Traditionally, it was felt that teachers should be firmly in control of the learning process, and that the teachers' task was to prepare and present material for students to understand. Within this approach, the relationship that students have with their teachers is not considered important, nor is the relationship that students have with each other in the classroom. Students' participation in class may be minimal, other than asking questions addressed to the teacher, or answering questions that the teacher referred to the student. This style encourages students to develop respect for positions of power as a source of control and discipline. It is often described as the formal authority model of teaching. A less rigid form of teacher-focused education is the protesters model. This maintains the teacher's conception of the formal authority model as a flashlight that illuminates the material for his class to learn, but emphasizes a more individualized approach to form. The demonstrator serves as both a role model and a guide, demonstrating skills and processes and then helping students develop and apply them independently. Instructors attracted to the demo style are generally confident that their way of performing a task represents a good baseline model, but they are sensitive to different learning styles and expect to provide students with help on an individual basis. Many education researchers argue instead for student-centered learning, and suggest that the learning process is more successful when students are in control. Within the student-centric paradigm, the patrician style is popular. The supervising teacher retains overall authority, but they delegate much of the responsibility for learning to the classroom as a way for students to become independent thinkers who take pride in their own work. Students are often encouraged to work on their own or in groups, and if the patrician style is successfully applied, they will build not only working knowledge on course-specific topics, but also self-discipline and the ability to coordinate group work and interpersonal roles. Another style that emphasizes student-centered education is the instructive mode of learning. Here, while a set of specific curriculum requirements already exists, students are encouraged to take initiative in creating ways to meet these learning requirements together. The teacher typically designs activities that encourage active learning, group collaboration, and problem-solving, and students are encouraged to process and implement course content in creative and original ways. While the delegated style emphasizes the content and responsibility that students have to produce and direct their knowledge base, the facilitator style emphasizes the form and the flowing and diverse possibilities that exist in the learning process. By the 1960s formal authority was widespread in almost all Western schools and universities. When a professor would enter a university lecture hall, one would expect a student to run, take his bag to the desk and pull out the chair the professor could sit on. This style has become obsolete over time. Now at university, students and professors typically have calmer, more collegial relationships, addressing each other on a first-name basis and recognizing that students have a lot to contribute in the classroom. However, teacher-focused education has a lasting appeal in the form of the demonstrative style, which remains useful in professions where skills must be demonstrated at an external level and the learning process remains constant in the early years of education. A student of mathematics, sewing or metalwork will most likely be familiar with the demonstrator style. At the highest levels of education, however, the demonstration approach should be abandoned in all areas as students are required to produce innovative work that makes a unique contribution to knowledge. Thesis students and doctoral students lead their own research in relief with supervisors. The patrician style is valuable when the course may lead students into careers that require group projects. Often, someone who has a high level of expertise in a particular field does not become the best employee because he has not learned to apply his abilities in a coordinated way. The patrician style tackles this problem by recognizing that interpersonal communication is not just a means of learning but an important skill in itself. The facilitator model is probably the most creative model, and therefore is not suitable for subjects where the practical component requires a very careful and disciplined way, such as training to become a doctor. However, it may suit more experimental and theoretical fields ranging from English, music and social sciences to science and medical research taking place in research laboratories. In these areas errors of form are important and valuable aspects of the learning and development process. Overall, there has been a clear evolution in the West from a rigid, dogmatic and teacher-dominated way of learning to a flexible, creative and student-centered approach. However, different subjects, ages and skill levels suit different teaching styles, and it is unlikely that there will ever be one recommended approach for all.
hypothesis: The formal authority model remains popular in the educational institutions of the West
label: c

Whether academic research really produces anything useful for the practice of business, or even whether its function is to do so, are questions that can provoke vigorous debate on campus. The debate, which first flared during the 1950s, was reignited in August when AACSB International, the most recognized global accreditation agency for business schools, announced that it would consider changing how it evaluates research. The news came in the wake of fairly scathing criticism in 2002 from Jeffrey Peppler. Stanford professor, and Christina Fong of the University of Washington, who questioned whether business education in its current guise is sustainable. The study found that traditional academy bikes do not adequately prepare students for the type of careers they face in the current period. The most controversial recommendation in the draft AACSBs report (sent to principals for their comment) is that schools should be required to demonstrate the value of their faculties research not only by listing its citations in journals, but by demonstrating the impact it has in the professional world. New qualifications, such as average income, student placement in leading companies and business collaborations will now be considered just as important than academic publications. The AACSB justifies its position by saying it wants schools and faculty to play to their strengths, be they in pedagogy, practical application research or scholarly endeavor. Traditionally, universities operate in a pyramid structure. Everyone enters and stays trying to succeed in their academic field. A psychology professor must publish competitive research in the leading neuroscience journals. A professor of cultural studies must send graduate students on new field research campaigns to be taken seriously. This research is the core of university output. And research of any kind is expensive. The AACSB points out that business schools in America alone spend more than $320 million a year on it. So it seems legitimate to ask, for what purpose is this done? If a school chooses to specialize in professional outputs rather than academic outputs, it can use such a large amount of money and redirect it to more fruitful programs. For example, if a business school wanted a greater presence of employees at leading financial firms, that money might be better invested in a career center focused on building the skills of students, rather than paying for higher-level research to be done through the effort of faculty. A change in assessment could also open the door to inviting more professionals from different disciplines to teach as adjuncts. Students can take accredited courses from people currently working in their dream field. The AACSB insists that universities answer the question of why research is the most critical component of traditional education. On one level, the question is simple to answer. Research in business schools, as everywhere else, is about expanding the boundaries of knowledge; it thrives on answering questions that haven't been asked. Certainly the pursuit of knowledge is still important to the university system. Our society advances because we learn how to do things in new ways, a process that is highly dependent on research and academia. But the other obvious practical uses of research publications cannot be ignored. Research is also concerned with building reputations for schools and professors. Schools gain fame from the publication records of their faculties: which journals publish them and how often. In some cases, as in government-funded schools in the UK, it can affect how much money they receive. For professors, the mantra is often publish or die. Their careers depend on them being seen in the right journals. But at some point, one has to wonder whether this research is being done for the benefit of the university or for the students the university aims to teach. Larger publications will attract more funding, which in turn will be invested into better publications. An article in a 2006 issue of Strategy and Leadership remarked that the study is not designed with managers' needs in mind, nor is it delivered in the journals they read. Most often, it has become a self-referential closed system with no relevance to organizational performance. The AACSB demands that this separation must change for the future of higher education. If students must invest thousands of dollars into education as part of their career trajectory, the academics who serve the students need to be more fully integrated into the professional world. This means universities must focus on other strengths outside research, such as professional networks, technological skills and relationships with leading business companies around the world. Although many universities opposed the report, today's world continues to change. Universities that prepare students for our changing future have no choice but to change with new trends and new standards.

The futile search for the cause of the rise in illiteracy is a tragic example of saying they can't see the tree for the trees. When teachers use picture books, they are simply continuing a long-standing tradition that is unquestionably accepted. And in the past two decades, illustrations in reading primers have become impoverished - sometimes to the point of extinction. Remarkably, there is almost no empirical evidence to support the use of illustrations in reading instruction. On the contrary, much empirical evidence shows that images detrimentally interfere with all aspects of reading learning. Even so, from North America to the Antipodes, the first books that many schoolchildren receive are completely text-free. The primary concern of the teacher is to help young beginning readers develop not only the ability to recognize words, but the skills necessary to understand what these words mean. Even if a child is able to read aloud fluently, he or she may not be able to understand much of it; this is called text barking. The teacher's task of improving understanding is hampered by influences outside the classroom. But the negative effects of things like TV, video games, or limited language experiences at home can be offset by a rich language experience at school. Instead, it's unusual that a book of 30 pages or more has only one sentence filled with repeated phrases. The works of art are often miraculous, but the pictures make the language superfluous, and children do not need to imagine anything when reading such books. Observing the image actively prevents children under the age of nine from forming a mental image, and can make it difficult for older children. In order to learn how to understand, they need to practice creating their own meaning in response to the text. They need to train their innate powers of imagination. As they get older, many children turn aside image-free numbers, and it's a situation that gets more severe as our culture becomes more visual. It's hard to wean children from picture books when images have played a major role during their formative reading experiences, and when there is competition for their attention from so many other sources of entertainment. The least intelligent are the most vulnerable, but tests show that even intelligent children are affected. The response of educators was to expand the use of images in books and simplify the language, even at senior levels. But motivation for reading should be provided by listening to well-read stories, where children imagine in response to the story. Then, when they start reading, they have this experience to help them understand the language. If we present pictures to save children the trouble of developing these creative skills, then I think we are making a big mistake. Academic journals ranging from educational research, psychology, language study, psycholinguistics, and so on point out experiments that demonstrate how harmful images are to beginning readers. Below is a brief selection: The results of the study by Canadian educationalist Dale Willow were clear and consistent: Images affected speed and accuracy and the closer the pictures were to words, the slower and more accurate the child's reading became. She argues that when children come to a word they already know, then the images are unnecessary and distracting. If they do not recognize a word and look in the image for a clue to its meaning, they may be misled by aspects of the images that are not closely related to the meaning of the word they are trying to understand. Jay Samuels, an American psychologist, found that poor readers who did not receive pictures learned words significantly more than those who learned to read with books with pictures. He examined the work of other researchers who reported problems using images and found that a word without a picture is better than a word plus a picture. When children were given words and pictures, those who seemed to ignore the pictures and pointed to the words learned more words than the children who pointed to the pictures, but they still learned fewer words than the children who had no illustrated stimuli at all.

Without language, we would never have been able to embark on our ascent to an unparalleled power over all other animals, and even nature itself. But language is first and foremost not just because it comes first. In itself it is an instrument of extraordinary ingenuity, but based on an idea of ingenious simplicity: this marvelous invention of composing from twenty-five or thirty sounds an infinite variety of expressions, which, although having in themselves no resemblance to what is in our minds, allow us to reveal to others its whole secret, and to inform those who cannot penetrate it all that we imagine, and the whole awakening that arises The nature of our soul. Thus, in 1660, the renowned French grammarians at the abbey of Port-Royal near Versailles distilled the essence of language, and since then no one has more eloquently celebrated the magnitude of its achievement. Nevertheless, there is only one flaw in all these hymns of praise, as the gesture of achievement unique to languages conceals a simple but critical discrepancy. Language is man's greatest invention, except, of course, that it was never invented. This apparent paradox is at the base of our fascination with language, and it holds many of its secrets. The language often seems so skillfully articulated that it can hardly be imagined as anything other than the perfect handiwork of a master craftsman. How else could this tool have derived so much out of barely three dozen lame bits of sound? By themselves, these formations of the mouth p, f, b, v, t, d, k, g, sh, a, e and so on amount to no more than a few spits and sprinkles of acrid, random noises with no meaning, no ability to express, no power to explain. But pass them through the cogs and wheels of the language machine, let it arrange them in some very special orders, and there is nothing that these insignificant streams of air cannot do: from the sigh of the endless boredom of existence to the unraveling of the basic order of the universe. However, the most unusual thing about language is that a person does not need to be a genius to drive his wheels. The language machine allows just about anyone, from pre-modern sponges in the subtropical savannah, to postmodern philosophers in suburban sprawl to tie these meaningless sounds to an infinite variety of subtle senses, all apparently without the slightest effort. But it is precisely this deceptive ease that makes the language a victim of its success, since in everyday life its triumphs are usually taken for granted. The wheels of language run so smoothly that one rarely bothers to stop and think about all the resourcefulness and expertise that must have been invested in making it function. Language hides art. Often, only alienation to foreign tongues, with their many exotic and strange features, brings home the wonder of language design. One of the most flamboyant stunts that some languages can perform is the ability to construct words of breathtaking length, thus expressing in one word what English takes an entire sentence to say. A Sumerian word like munintumaa (when made appropriate for it) might seem rather chopped up compared to the Turkish colossus above. What is so impressive about it, however, is not its length but, on the contrary, the economical compactness of its construction. This sleek design allows individual sounds to convey useful information, and in fact even the absence of a tone enlisted to express something specific. Often there are sanctions outlined for any violation of this compromise. The second way companies often resolve disputes between employees is through the assistive approach. This method encourages open communication, identifying common ground and encouraging the parties to the conflict themselves to find a solution, rather than a third party.
